4-1.title: Consistent Verb Tense
4-1.learn:
HOW TO KEEP VERB TENSE CONSISTENT

Tense shows WHEN something happens: past (walked), present (walks), or future (will walk). Keep your verbs in the SAME time frame unless the timing really changes.

Example 1 — Inconsistent: 'She walks into the room and grabbed her coat.'
'Walks' is present, but 'grabbed' is past. They don't match. Fix to all past: 'She walked into the room and grabbed her coat.' OR all present: 'She walks into the room and grabs her coat.'

Example 2 — Consistent past: 'He opened the door, looked outside, and smiled.'
All three verbs (opened, looked, smiled) are past tense, so it flows.

Example 3 — When a change IS okay: 'Yesterday I studied, and tomorrow I will take the test.'
Here the time really changes from past to future, so different tenses are correct.

To check: read your sentence and find every verb. If they bounce between past and present by accident, pick one tense and make them all match.

questions.question: Which sentence keeps verb tense consistent?

choices.A: He runs to the store and bought milk.
choices.B: He ran to the store and buys milk.
choices.C: He ran to the store and bought milk.
choices.D: He run to the store and buy milk.

questions.explanation: Both 'ran' and 'bought' are past tense, so the tense stays consistent.

questions.question: Which sentence has a tense SHIFT error?

choices.A: She sings and dances every night.
choices.B: She sang and danced last night.
choices.C: She sings and danced last night.
choices.D: She will sing and dance tonight.

questions.explanation: 'Sings' is present but 'danced' is past, creating an incorrect tense shift.

questions.question: Fix the tense: 'The dog barked loudly and ___ at the mail carrier.'
questions.explanation: To match the past-tense 'barked,' use the past-tense 'jumped.'

questions.question: Which revision corrects 'I wake up early and made breakfast.'?

choices.A: I wake up early and made breakfast.
choices.B: I woke up early and made breakfast.
choices.C: I woke up early and make breakfast.
choices.D: I wake up early and making breakfast.

questions.explanation: Changing 'wake' to 'woke' makes both verbs past tense and consistent.

questions.question: Which sentence is consistently in PRESENT tense?

choices.A: The chef chops the vegetables and cooked the soup.
choices.B: The chef chops the vegetables and cooks the soup.
choices.C: The chef chopped the vegetables and cooks the soup.
choices.D: The chef chop the vegetables and cook the soup.

questions.explanation: Both 'chops' and 'cooks' are present tense, so the sentence is consistent.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses DIFFERENT tenses because the time really changes?

choices.A: Yesterday she studied, and tomorrow she will take the test.
choices.B: She studies yesterday and took the test tomorrow.
choices.C: She walks home and grabbed her keys.
choices.D: He jumps the fence and landed hard.

questions.explanation: The time genuinely shifts from past ('yesterday') to future ('tomorrow'), so the different tenses are correct.

questions.question: Which verb keeps the tense consistent: 'She opened the book, read a page, and ___ it down.'
questions.explanation: To match 'opened' and 'read' (past), use the past-tense 'set.'

questions.question: Which paragraph keeps tense consistent throughout?

choices.A: The hero enters the cave. He found a treasure and runs out.
choices.B: The hero entered the cave. He found a treasure and ran out.
choices.C: The hero enters the cave. He finds a treasure and ran out.
choices.D: The hero entered the cave. He finds a treasure and runs out.

questions.explanation: All the verbs (entered, found, ran) are past tense, so the paragraph stays consistent.

questions.question: Which sentence should be corrected for a tense shift?

choices.A: When the storm hit, the lights flickered and went out.
choices.B: When the storm hits, the lights flicker and go out.
choices.C: When the storm hit, the lights flicker and went out.
choices.D: When the storm hits, the lights will flicker and go out.

questions.explanation: Choice C mixes past ('hit,' 'went') with present ('flicker'), which is an incorrect shift.

questions.question: Choose the BEST revision: 'As the team practices, they worked hard and improve.'

choices.A: As the team practices, they work hard and improve.
choices.B: As the team practiced, they work hard and improve.
choices.C: As the team practices, they worked hard and improved.
choices.D: As the team practice, they working hard and improve.

questions.explanation: Making all verbs present tense (practices, work, improve) fixes the shift consistently.

4-2.title: Subject-Verb Agreement
4-2.learn:
HOW TO MAKE SUBJECTS AND VERBS AGREE

A SINGULAR subject needs a singular verb; a PLURAL subject needs a plural verb. In present tense, a singular verb often ends in -s, while the plural form does not.

Example 1 — 'The dog runs.' / 'The dogs run.'
One dog = 'runs' (singular verb). Many dogs = 'run' (plural verb).

Example 2 — Watch for words BETWEEN the subject and verb: 'The box of crayons IS on the desk.'
The subject is 'box' (singular), NOT 'crayons.' So the verb is 'is,' not 'are.' Ignore the prepositional phrase 'of crayons' when choosing the verb.

Example 3 — Compound subjects with 'and' are plural: 'Sam and Maria walk to school.'
Two people joined by 'and' take the plural verb 'walk.'

Tip: Find the TRUE subject first (cross out any 'of ___' phrases), decide if it's singular or plural, then match the verb.

questions.question: Choose the correct verb: 'The cat ___ on the windowsill.'
questions.explanation: The singular subject 'cat' takes the singular verb 'sits.'

questions.question: Choose the correct verb: 'The students ___ in the hallway.'
questions.explanation: The plural subject 'students' takes the plural verb 'wait.'

questions.question: Choose the correct verb: 'My friend ___ soccer every day.'
questions.explanation: The singular subject 'friend' takes the singular verb 'plays.'

questions.question: Choose the correct verb: 'The box of markers ___ on the table.'
questions.explanation: The true subject is 'box' (singular), not 'markers,' so the verb is 'is.'

questions.question: Choose the correct verb: 'Sam and Maria ___ to the same school.'
questions.explanation: Two subjects joined by 'and' are plural, so they take the plural verb 'go.'

questions.question: Choose the correct verb: 'The bowl of apples ___ fresh.'
questions.explanation: The subject is 'bowl' (singular), not 'apples,' so use the singular verb 'looks.'

questions.question: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?

choices.A: The team of players are ready.
choices.B: The list of names were long.
choices.C: The group of friends is happy.
choices.D: The pair of shoes are new.

questions.explanation: 'Group' is the singular subject, so 'is' agrees with it; the others wrongly use plural verbs.

questions.question: Choose the correct verb: 'Each of the players ___ a uniform.'
questions.explanation: 'Each' is singular, so it takes the singular verb 'has,' ignoring 'of the players.'

questions.question: Which sentence is correct?

choices.A: Neither the dogs nor the cat are hungry.
choices.B: Neither the dogs nor the cat is hungry.
choices.C: Neither the dogs nor the cat be hungry.
choices.D: Neither the dogs nor the cat were hungry.

questions.explanation: With 'neither/nor,' the verb agrees with the closer subject 'cat' (singular), so 'is' is correct.

questions.question: Choose the correct verb: 'There ___ several reasons for the delay.'
questions.explanation: The real subject is the plural 'reasons,' so the verb is 'are.'

4-3.title: Active vs. Passive Voice
4-3.learn:
HOW TO TELL ACTIVE FROM PASSIVE VOICE

In ACTIVE voice, the subject DOES the action: 'The chef cooked the meal.' (chef = doer, comes first)
In PASSIVE voice, the subject RECEIVES the action: 'The meal was cooked by the chef.' (meal = receiver, doer comes last or is missing)

Example 1 — Active: 'The dog chased the ball.'
The subject 'dog' does the chasing. Strong and direct.

Example 2 — Passive: 'The ball was chased by the dog.'
The subject 'ball' receives the action. It uses a 'be' verb (was) + past participle (chased), often with 'by.'

Example 3 — Spotting passive: look for a form of 'be' (is, was, were, been) + a past-participle verb, and ask 'who did it?' If the doer comes after 'by' (or is missing), it's passive.
Active: 'Maria wrote the letter.' Passive: 'The letter was written by Maria.'
Active voice is usually clearer and stronger, so prefer it in most writing.

questions.question: Which sentence is in ACTIVE voice?

choices.B: The cake was eaten by the kids.

questions.explanation: In 'The kids ate the cake,' the subject 'kids' does the action, so it is active.

questions.question: Which sentence is in PASSIVE voice?

choices.B: The mural was painted by the artist.
choices.D: The artist will paint a mural.

questions.explanation: In 'The mural was painted by the artist,' the subject 'mural' receives the action, so it is passive.

questions.question: In active voice, what does the subject do?
questions.explanation: In active voice, the subject performs or does the action.

questions.question: Which is the ACTIVE version of 'The window was broken by the storm.'?

choices.D: The storm was broken by the window.

questions.explanation: Making the doer 'the storm' the subject creates the active sentence 'The storm broke the window.'

questions.question: Which is the PASSIVE version of 'The teacher graded the tests.'?

choices.C: The tests were graded by the teacher.

questions.explanation: Making the receiver 'the tests' the subject creates the passive 'The tests were graded by the teacher.'

questions.question: What clue helps you spot passive voice?

choices.A: A form of 'be' (is, was, were) plus a past-participle verb

questions.explanation: Passive voice uses a 'be' verb plus a past participle, often with 'by' naming the doer.

questions.question: Which sentence is ACTIVE?

choices.B: The package was delivered by the driver.

questions.explanation: In choice C, the subject 'driver' performs the action, making it active.

questions.question: Why is active voice usually preferred?

choices.C: It hides who did the action.

questions.explanation: Active voice is usually clearer and more direct because the doer comes first.

questions.question: Which sentence is in PASSIVE voice?

choices.D: The tree was struck by lightning.

questions.explanation: In choice D, the subject 'tree' receives the action and uses 'was struck by,' making it passive.

questions.question: Rewrite in active voice: 'The trophy was awarded to the winner by the judges.'

choices.B: The judges awarded the trophy to the winner.
choices.C: The winner was awarded the trophy.

questions.explanation: Making the doer 'the judges' the subject creates the active sentence.

4-4.title: Verb Mood
4-4.learn:
HOW TO IDENTIFY VERB MOOD

Mood shows the PURPOSE of a verb. The three main moods are:
INDICATIVE — states a fact or asks a question: 'It is raining.' / 'Are you ready?'
IMPERATIVE — gives a command or request: 'Close the window.' (The subject 'you' is understood.)
SUBJUNCTIVE — shows a wish or something not real/contrary to fact: 'If I were taller, I'd dunk.' Notice 'were,' not 'was,' in a wish.

Example 1 — Indicative: 'The sun rises in the east.'
It simply states a fact, so the mood is indicative.

Example 2 — Imperative: 'Please sit down.'
It gives a command. The subject 'you' is understood, so the mood is imperative.

Example 3 — Subjunctive: 'I wish I were a bird.'
It expresses a wish about something untrue. The subjunctive uses 'were' (not 'was') even with 'I.'
Key clue: commands = imperative; facts/questions = indicative; wishes or 'if I were' = subjunctive.

questions.question: Which sentence is in the IMPERATIVE mood (a command)?
questions.explanation: 'Close the door' gives a command, so it is imperative.

questions.question: Which sentence is in the INDICATIVE mood (states a fact)?

choices.B: If I were rich, I'd travel.

questions.explanation: 'The bus arrives at noon' states a fact, so it is indicative.

questions.question: Which mood gives a command?
questions.explanation: The imperative mood gives commands or requests.

questions.question: Which sentence is in the SUBJUNCTIVE mood (a wish or unreal idea)?

choices.C: If I were you, I would apologize.

questions.explanation: 'If I were you' expresses an unreal condition, using the subjunctive 'were.'

questions.question: Choose the correct subjunctive verb: 'I wish I ___ taller.'
questions.explanation: The subjunctive uses 'were' (not 'was') to express a wish or unreal situation.

questions.question: What is the understood subject of an imperative sentence like 'Clean your room'?
questions.explanation: In a command, the subject 'you' is understood even though it is not written.

questions.question: Which sentence is INDICATIVE?

choices.A: If he were here, he would help.
choices.D: I wish I had more time.

questions.explanation: 'It snowed all night long' states a fact, making it indicative.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses the subjunctive mood?

choices.A: If I was president, I would lower taxes.
choices.B: If I were president, I would lower taxes.
choices.C: If I am president, I would lower taxes.
choices.D: If I be president, I would lower taxes.

questions.explanation: An unreal 'if' statement uses the subjunctive 'were,' not 'was.'

questions.question: Identify the mood: 'Please pass the salt.'
questions.explanation: It makes a polite request/command, so the mood is imperative.

questions.question: Which sentence shows a wish using the subjunctive?

choices.C: I wish I were on vacation.

questions.explanation: 'I wish I were on vacation' expresses a wish about something not real, using the subjunctive 'were.'

4-5.title: Verbals: Gerunds, Infinitives & Participles
4-5.learn:
HOW TO RECOGNIZE VERBALS

Verbals are verb forms that act as OTHER parts of speech. There are three kinds:
GERUND — ends in -ing and acts as a NOUN: 'Swimming is fun.' (Swimming is the subject, a noun.)
INFINITIVE — is 'to + verb' and often acts as a noun: 'I want to swim.' (to swim = what I want)
PARTICIPLE — a verb form (often -ing or -ed) that acts as an ADJECTIVE to describe a noun: 'the swimming pool,' 'the broken cup.'

Example 1 — Gerund: 'Running keeps me healthy.'
'Running' ends in -ing and acts as a noun (the subject), so it is a gerund.

Example 2 — Infinitive: 'She loves to read.'
'To read' is 'to + verb' and names what she loves, so it is an infinitive.

Example 3 — Participle: 'The barking dog scared me.'
'Barking' describes the noun 'dog,' so it is a participle (acting as an adjective).

Key test: Is the -ing word a NOUN (gerund) or describing a noun (participle)? Is it 'to + verb' (infinitive)?

questions.question: What is the gerund in this sentence? 'Swimming is great exercise.'
questions.explanation: 'Swimming' ends in -ing and acts as a noun (the subject), so it is a gerund.

questions.question: What is the infinitive in this sentence? 'I want to learn guitar.'
questions.explanation: 'To learn' is 'to + verb,' which makes it an infinitive.

questions.question: Which word is a participle (describing a noun)? 'The broken window let in cold air.'
questions.explanation: 'Broken' is a participle describing the noun 'window,' acting like an adjective.

questions.question: Which sentence contains a GERUND?
questions.explanation: In choice B, 'Dancing' acts as a noun (the subject), making it a gerund.

questions.question: Which sentence contains an INFINITIVE?

choices.A: She hopes to travel this summer.

questions.explanation: 'To travel' is 'to + verb,' which is an infinitive.

questions.question: Which sentence uses '-ing' word as a PARTICIPLE (describing a noun)?

choices.C: The singing birds woke me up.
choices.D: Singing is good for the soul.

questions.explanation: In 'the singing birds,' 'singing' describes the noun 'birds,' so it is a participle.

questions.question: In 'Jogging every morning improves your health,' what role does 'Jogging' play?

choices.A: A gerund acting as the subject (a noun)
choices.B: A verb showing the main action

questions.explanation: 'Jogging' is the subject of the sentence and acts as a noun, so it is a gerund.

questions.question: Which sentence contains a PARTICIPLE?

choices.A: To win the prize was her goal.
choices.D: The frightened cat hid under the bed.

questions.explanation: 'Frightened' describes the noun 'cat,' acting as an adjective, so it is a participle.

questions.question: Which sentence uses an -ing word as a GERUND, not a participle?

choices.C: Running is good for your heart.

questions.explanation: In 'Running is good for your heart,' 'Running' is the subject (a noun), so it is a gerund; the others describe nouns.

questions.question: Identify the verbal type: 'She decided to volunteer at the shelter.'
questions.explanation: 'To volunteer' is 'to + verb,' which makes it an infinitive.
